lesson.title: Three Threads, One Explanation: The Biopsychosocial Model
lesson.summary: The biopsychosocial model explains health and psychological disorders as the product of biological, psychological, and social factors acting together, rather than looking for any single cause.
lesson.body:
Physician George Engel proposed the biopsychosocial model in 1977 as a direct challenge to the purely biomedical model of illness that dominated medicine at the time, a model that tended to reduce illness, including mental illness, to biological malfunction alone. Engel argued that a full account of health, whether physical or psychological, has to include psychological and social dimensions as well as biological ones.

The model names three interacting components. Biological factors include genetics, neurochemistry, brain structure and function, and physical health conditions. Psychological factors include thought patterns, coping style, personality traits, learned behaviors, and emotion regulation. Social factors include relationships, family environment, culture, socioeconomic status, access to resources, and life stressors or sources of support. The model's central claim is that these three domains interact rather than simply operating side by side: a social stressor, for example, can alter biological stress hormones, which can shape a person's psychological capacity to cope, which then affects how they engage socially, in an ongoing loop rather than a one-directional chain.

This connects directly back to the difficulty of defining a psychological disorder. Just as no single criterion, distress, dysfunction, deviance, or danger, fully captures what makes something a disorder, the biopsychosocial model makes a parallel argument about causation: simple, single-cause explanations for a psychological disorder, whether framed as purely genetic or purely a matter of upbringing, are almost always incomplete, because in most cases the evidence points to contributions from multiple domains acting together.

The model also offers a useful way to move past the old nature versus nurture framing. Rather than treating biological, nature-leaning factors and social or environmental, nurture-leaning factors as competing explanations where only one can be correct, the biopsychosocial model treats them as jointly operating alongside psychological processes. The next chapter looks at the diathesis-stress model, which can be understood as one specific, more mechanism-focused application of this broader biopsychosocial logic.
